question: Do small and medium open-weight language models reduce computational effort when a prompt asks for an everyday numerical estimate rather than an exact answer, and what do probes, pruning, and layer diagnostics suggest about the representations used for approximate versus exact arithmetic?

key_findings.claim: Author-reported: on the 1,000-item StreetMath benchmark, every tested architecture selected the exact-answer option more often than the designated good-approximation option except Qwen3-4B-Instruct, and Dream-v0-Instruct selected the exact answer on all 1,000 items.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports good-approximation versus exact-math counts of 445 versus 514 for Qwen3-4B-Instruct, 151 versus 637 for Qwen3-4B-Thinking, 0 versus 1,000 for Dream-v0-Instruct, 177 versus 469 for Falcon-Mamba, and 174 versus 459 for Mamba-GPT. Average generated-token counts are 125, 228, 263, 131, and 86 respectively. These are preference-category counts, not ordinary answer-accuracy scores: the benchmark treats its handcrafted approximate option as correct and an exact numerical answer as a separate, undesired category.

anchors.section: Appendix B.2, benchmark labels and metric

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: two central descriptions of the benchmark do not reconcile with the reported table.
key_findings.evidence: The protocol says any tool usage is flagged as exact math, but Table 1 reports 1,000 tool calls for Qwen3-4B-Instruct alongside only 514 exact-math judgments and 445 good-approximation judgments. The prose also says Qwen3-4B-Thinking has better approximation performance than Qwen3-4B-Instruct, while the table reports 151 versus 445 good approximations. Without released row-level reconciliation, neither statement follows from the displayed counts.

anchors.section: Appendix B.2, parser and judgment rules

key_findings.claim: Author-reported: a linear classifier can decode digit-form proximity to multiples of five or ten very accurately at some layer, whereas word-form transfer is substantially weaker.
key_findings.evidence: For near-five digits, best-layer accuracy ranges from 0.917 to 0.999; for near-ten digits it ranges from 0.967 to 0.999. With number words, near-five accuracy ranges from 0.603 to 0.784 and near-ten from 0.680 to 0.811. The study trains on Template A digits, tests prompt transfer on Template B digits, and tests surface-form transfer on Template A words using 4,000 train and 1,500 validation samples per condition.

anchors.section: Section 3, Linear Probe on Rounding Behaviors
Appendix C.1-C.2, probe data and evaluation

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the word-form probe results do not by themselves demonstrate a learned abstract rounding concept because several headline accuracies are at or near a trivial class-frequency baseline.
key_findings.evidence: The near-five definition labels six of ten terminal digits positive, making an always-positive classifier about 60% accurate under uniform sampling; the reported Qwen and Dream word accuracies are 0.603, 0.607, and 0.620. Near-ten labels three of ten terminal digits positive, making an always-negative classifier about 70% accurate; reported word accuracies are 0.680-0.811. The paper reports accuracy but no balanced accuracy, AUROC, class-matched baseline, confidence interval, or repeated seed, and Table 4 shows 94.3-100% error in the distance-2+ bucket for three models.

key_findings.claim: Author-reported: masks selected from math-calibration activations can leave StreetMath performance stable or improve it at some sparsity settings while GSM8K accuracy collapses to near zero.
key_findings.evidence: The MathNeuro adaptation ranks linear-layer weights using activation magnitude times weight magnitude over 200 calibration samples and evaluates masks over nine proportions. Figure 2 shows highly non-monotonic StreetMath curves for most models and an all-but-zero GSM8K curve. The appendix discloses that each setting is run once, uses bootstrap samples of at most 500 calibration/evaluation examples, caps tasks at 1,000 items, truncates prompts to 256 tokens, and counts only the good-approximation category as correct on StreetMath.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the pruning experiment supports a task-dependent sensitivity result, but not the stronger claim that exact and approximate arithmetic occupy separate neural components.
key_findings.evidence: There is no unpruned zero-mask baseline in Figure 2, the text alternates between a keep-mask retaining the top p percent and an x-axis labeled proportion pruned, every setting is a single run, and StreetMath and GSM8K differ in prompts, answer formats, length, scoring, and dataset distribution. MathNeuro's source method explicitly filters math-specific parameters against general-language importance, whereas this paper's short method description only states magnitude accumulation, leaving the isolation contrast unclear. These confounds can create divergent pruning curves without demonstrating disjoint circuits.

anchors.section: Section 4, mask construction and dual-pathway interpretation
Figure 2, pruning axes and task curves
Appendix D, one-run and capped-evaluation protocol

key_findings.claim: Author-reported: layerwise spectral entropy and effective rank often follow a high-low-high trajectory, with StreetMath exhibiting greater late-layer expansion and transition distances than GSM8K for the same model.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 3-7 compare spectral entropy, effective rank, activation entropy, cosine similarity, L2 distance, angular distance, covariance trace, gradient proxy, and logit-lens proxy across layers. The authors interpret comparable elbow depths as evidence that approximation does not shorten computation and the StreetMath/GSM8K difference as consistent with broader versus narrower neuron use. The appendix aggregates per-prompt means and sample standard deviations over at most 1,000 examples at the modal vector length.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the paper establishes behavior under one constructed multiple-choice preference test, not human-machine cognitive-miserliness equivalence or a universal failure to approximate.
key_findings.evidence: StreetMath supplies one deterministic good option, penalizes the exact option even though it is numerically within the stated 20% tolerance, and uses token count as the sole effort proxy. Models receive architecture-specific prompts, Qwen3-4B-Instruct can call tools, and inference latency, FLOPs, energy, confidence, free-response estimate quality, and human baselines are not reported. The authors themselves limit scope to 1,000 simple-arithmetic items and five small/medium open models.

method.core_idea: Construct a 1,000-item, five-topic multiple-choice benchmark whose options separate an exact result from one deterministic acceptable estimate and two large-error distractors; compare five open-weight architectures, then probe number proximity, prune calibration-selected parameters, and contrast layerwise diagnostics between StreetMath and GSM8K.
method.mechanism: The behavioral test classifies generated choices and traces as good approximation, exact math, mildly off, or way off while counting tokens and tool calls. Probes test linear decodability of proximity to multiples of five or ten. Weight-activation masks intervene on parameters associated with math calibration data, and hidden-state spectra and inter-layer distances serve as descriptive proxies for representational breadth and computational transitions.
assumptions: A single deterministic rounded option captures the range of contextually reasonable human estimates for each item.
Selecting an exact option is evidence of wasted cognitive effort even when the model may retrieve or recognize it directly.
Generated-token count is a comparable proxy for computation across autoregressive, state-space, thinking, and diffusion architectures.
Architecture-specific prompt adaptations do not confound cross-model comparisons.
The output parser distinguishes exact computation, approximation, malformed output, and tool use consistently across backends.
Multiple-choice selection behavior transfers to free-response, real-world estimation.
A best-layer linear probe trained on one prompt family measures a represented numerical concept rather than class imbalance, token identity, or template artifacts.
Activation-times-weight magnitude on 200 calibration samples isolates exact-math parameters sufficiently for a causal pathway claim.
Differences between pruned GSM8K and StreetMath performance are neural-task differences rather than scoring, prompt, length, or distribution differences.
Spectral entropy, effective rank, covariance trace, and adjacent-layer distance correspond to cognitive effort and breadth of neuron use.
At most 1,000 examples and one run per pruning/probing setting are adequate despite no uncertainty intervals.
The five 3B-7B open models are informative about LLM approximation behavior beyond the evaluated checkpoints.

techniques.role: Generates exact, designated-good, mildly-off, and way-off answer options across baskets, discounts, taxes, units, and tips.
Parses choices, numerical answers, short reasoning, optional think blocks, tool calls, tokens, and latency into behavioral categories.
Compares two Qwen variants, a diffusion LM, and two state-space models under locally adapted prompts.
Tests whether hidden states linearly expose proximity to multiples of five or ten across digit templates and number words.
Ranks linear-layer parameters using calibration activations and weight magnitudes, then masks selected proportions before task evaluation.
Tracks spectral entropy, effective rank, activation entropy, covariance trace, and proxy gradients through model depth.
Uses cosine similarity, L2 distance, and angular distance to compare representational change on StreetMath and GSM8K.

evaluations.setting: All 1,000 StreetMath multiple-choice items over five topics; Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, Falcon-Mamba-7B-Instruct, and Mamba-GPT-3B.
evaluations.metric: Counts of designated good approximation, exact math, mild/large error, tool calls, and average generated tokens.
evaluations.result: Good/exact counts are 445/514, 151/637, 0/1,000, 177/469, and 174/459; average tokens are 125, 228, 263, 131, and 86. Qwen3-4B-Instruct is reported with 1,000 tool calls despite only 514 exact labels.
evaluations.baseline: Cross-model comparison under adapted prompts; no human, random-choice, free-response, equal-FLOP, or exact-answer-as-valid baseline is reported.

evaluations.setting: StreetMath topic breakdown for basket sum, discounts, taxes, units, and tips.
evaluations.result: Dream selects exact on every item in every topic. Qwen3-4B-Instruct's good-approximation counts are 86, 15, 40, 22, and 22, while Qwen3-4B-Thinking's are 46, 80, 40, 35, and 28; these topic results further show that neither Qwen checkpoint uniformly dominates the other.
evaluations.baseline: The exact-answer and three non-exact option categories generated by the benchmark.

evaluations.setting: Near-five digit probing with 4,000 training and 1,500 validation samples per condition, best layer selected separately per model.
evaluations.metric: Best-layer classification accuracy and error by distance bucket.
evaluations.result: Peak accuracy is 0.939, 0.917, 0.970, 0.989, and 0.999. Best layers are 2, 6, 26, 7, and 3. Distance-bucket errors vary and do not support a universal distance-one-hardest rule.
evaluations.baseline: Same probe transferred from Template A digits to Template B digits; no explicit majority or balanced-class baseline.

evaluations.setting: Number-word transfer for the near-five and near-ten probes.
evaluations.result: Near-five word accuracy is 0.603-0.784 and near-ten word accuracy is 0.680-0.811. Three models make 94.3-100% error on near-five distance-2+ examples; near-ten errors for exact/distance-one word cases reach 96-100% for three transformer/diffusion models.
evaluations.baseline: Implicit class-frequency baselines are approximately 0.60 for near-five and 0.70 for near-ten under uniform terminal digits, but the paper does not report them.

evaluations.setting: Nine activation-weight mask proportions, five models, StreetMath, GSM8K, MMLU, and RACE; one run per setting with capped samples.
evaluations.metric: Task accuracy versus the displayed pruning proportion.
evaluations.result: GSM8K remains near zero under the plotted masks, while StreetMath, MMLU, and RACE are often non-monotonic and sometimes improve at intermediate proportions. Qwen3-4B-Instruct is the clearest exception to the paper's stability/improvement summary.
evaluations.baseline: Other mask proportions and other tasks; Figure 2 does not display an unpruned zero-mask control.

evaluations.setting: Up to 1,000 GSM8K and StreetMath prompts per model, with hidden-state diagnostics aggregated at the most common series length.
evaluations.metric: Layerwise spectral entropy, effective rank, activation entropy, covariance trace, gradient proxy, logit-lens proxy, cosine similarity, L2 distance, and angular distance.
evaluations.result: Most plots show an early compression followed by later expansion; StreetMath often has larger late-layer entropy/rank and transition distances, with Falcon-Mamba on StreetMath identified as an exception.
evaluations.baseline: GSM8K on the same checkpoint, but input/output length, prompts, labels, and data distributions are not matched.

limitations: Author-stated: StreetMath contains only 1,000 problems and may not cover the variety of real-world estimation tasks.
Author-stated: only five small/medium open-source checkpoints are evaluated, so results may not generalize to larger proprietary models or other architectures.
Author-stated: the task is restricted to numerical approximation in simple arithmetic; more complex mathematical domains are untested.
Reviewer-identified: no human participants or human-estimation distribution support the cognitive-miserliness comparison, option construction, or 20% threshold.

Reviewer-identified: exact answers are scored as a separate undesired category even though they fall within any ordinary relative-error tolerance; the metric measures preference conformity, not simply approximation quality.
Reviewer-identified: Table 1's tool-call labels and the claimed Qwen Thinking advantage contradict the displayed counts.
Reviewer-identified: adapted prompts, tool access, generation styles, and tokenization differ across architectures, so raw token counts are not equal-compute measurements.
Reviewer-identified: probe accuracy is vulnerable to severe class imbalance, best-layer selection on the evaluation target, single-seed variance, and surface-form leakage.
Reviewer-identified: the pruning protocol is single-run, sample-capped, ambiguously labels keep versus prune proportions, and omits an unpruned baseline from the figure.
Reviewer-identified: pruning differences between GSM8K and StreetMath do not isolate exact versus approximate computation because task distributions, prompts, lengths, and scoring differ.
Reviewer-identified: layerwise spectra are descriptive and cannot establish neuron-set breadth, effort, or separate pathways without matched inputs and causal interventions.
Reviewer-identified: no confidence intervals, repeated model seeds, prompt sensitivity study, evaluator agreement, contamination audit, or robust row-level error analysis is reported.
failure_modes: A model can appear non-miserly by selecting an exact option from memorized or shallow pattern recognition without spending more inference compute.
A model can appear approximately capable by recognizing the benchmark's deterministic rounding templates rather than estimating flexibly.
The parser can label tool use, exact intermediate arithmetic, and a final approximate option inconsistently, as the Qwen3-4B-Instruct aggregate suggests.
A designated good estimate can be unnatural or suboptimal in context even though it is the only category counted as correct.
Thinking, diffusion, and state-space token counts are not directly comparable measures of latency, FLOPs, or energy.
A best-layer probe can exploit terminal-digit frequency or token identity and still look like numerical-topology representation.
Masking magnitude-ranked weights can alter general language, formatting, or multiple-choice calibration rather than selectively removing exact-arithmetic circuitry.
Single-run pruning improvements can be noise from sample resampling, prompt truncation, or non-monotonic decoding rather than denoising.
GSM8K-versus-StreetMath spectral differences can be driven by sequence length and lexical distribution rather than computation type.
Findings from 3B-7B open checkpoints may reverse for larger, tool-disabled, instruction-tuned, or calibrated systems.
reusable_insights: Approximation benchmarks should accept a distribution or interval of defensible estimates and report exact accuracy separately from effort-sensitive utility.
Compare reasoning efficiency with wall time, FLOPs, energy, and generated tokens; normalize architecture-specific decoding and tool use.
A cognitive analogy needs a matched human experiment rather than an assumed rounding rule.
Probe evaluations should report class frequencies, majority and shuffled-label controls, balanced accuracy or AUROC, held-out templates, and nested layer selection.
Circuit-separation claims require matched exact/approximate versions of the same problems, causal cross-task patches or ablations, and general-language controls.
Publish row-level parser decisions so aggregate tool-use, reasoning-trace, and final-choice labels can be reconciled.
Negative or contradictory aggregates are especially valuable when they constrain a broad behavioral conclusion.
open_questions: How do human participants distribute estimates, response time, and mental steps on the exact same StreetMath items?
Do conclusions persist when any estimate inside a context-specific interval earns credit and exact answers remain numerically valid?
What happens under matched tool-disabled prompts, temperature, latency, FLOPs, and energy across architectures?
Can row-level records explain why all 1,000 Qwen3-4B-Instruct outputs are counted as tool calls but fewer are labeled exact math?
Does the Qwen Thinking versus Instruct ranking change under a preregistered metric that resolves the Table 1/prose conflict?
Do balanced probes with held-out number ranges and adversarial digit/word tokenizations retain the reported near-five and near-ten signals?
Can paired exact/approximate paraphrases of identical arithmetic isolate causal components through activation patching and recovery tests?
Are pruning improvements replicated across seeds and an explicit unpruned checkpoint without prompt truncation?

competitive_landscape.title: Do LLMs Overthink Basic Math Reasoning? Benchmarking the Accuracy-Efficiency Tradeoff in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: LLMThinkBench evaluates 53 models on 14 dynamically generated basic-math tasks and combines correctness with token efficiency in an Overthinking Score. StreetMath instead makes approximation preference itself the target and adds probes, pruning, and cross-architecture diagnostics, but evaluates only five checkpoints.

competitive_landscape.title: Language Models Do Hard Arithmetic Tasks Easily and Hardly Do Easy Arithmetic Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Gambardella et al. contrast first- and last-digit multiplication behavior and confidence to show that apparent arithmetic difficulty is not computational difficulty. StreetMath instead contrasts exact-choice and approximate-choice behavior in everyday scenarios, making this work a warning that output preference need not reveal effort.

competitive_landscape.title: Language Models Encode Numbers Using Digit Representations in Base 10
competitive_landscape.difference: Levy and Geva use probing plus causal interventions to identify per-digit circular representations. StreetMath uses linear proximity probes across digit and word forms but provides no comparable causal intervention, then connects those weaker probes to approximation behavior.

competitive_landscape.title: GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: GSM-Symbolic perturbs numerical values and adds irrelevant clauses to measure robustness of exact reasoning. StreetMath creates approximation-specific option categories and studies efficiency, but does not perform the same template-instantiation, irrelevant-clause, or contamination robustness audit.

competitive_landscape.title: Math Neurosurgery: Isolating Language Models' Math Reasoning Abilities Using Only Forward Passes
competitive_landscape.relationship: source pruning method and direct circuit baseline
competitive_landscape.difference: MathNeuro explicitly identifies math-specific weights relative to general-language importance and validates deletion and scaling over math and non-math tasks. StreetMath adapts its activation-weight ranking to compare StreetMath and GSM8K, but the compressed protocol and single runs do not reproduce the same isolation guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: Pre-trained Large Language Models Use Fourier Features to Compute Addition
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhou et al. identify low-frequency magnitude and high-frequency modular-addition mechanisms with mechanistic experiments. StreetMath asks whether precision-oriented mechanisms impede estimation, but does not localize or causally contrast an approximation circuit at that resolution.

competitive_landscape.title: Break the Chain: Large Language Models Can be Shortcut Reasoners
competitive_landscape.difference: Break the Chain directly prompts heuristic shortcuts over arithmetic, logic, and commonsense tasks and evaluates whether shorter reasoning preserves performance. StreetMath instead diagnoses a failure to select approximation and uses designated rounded answers, without an intervention that trains or prompts the same model to switch strategies.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors present StreetMath as a new 1,000-item benchmark for everyday approximation, claim that diverse autoregressive, diffusion, and state-space LMs prefer exact computation over effort-saving estimates, and argue from probing, pruning, and layer diagnostics that exact and approximate arithmetic use different neural pathways.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The benchmark spans five scenario families and five open checkpoints, with category counts, token counts, digit/word proximity probes, nine mask proportions, and layerwise metrics. Appendices provide generation rules, model/hardware details, probe definitions, single-run pruning constraints, layer aggregation, broad related work, and stated limitations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the combination of an approximation-preference benchmark with cross-architecture behavioral counts and preliminary interpretability diagnostics. The evidence does not establish universal cognitive miserliness or separate neural circuits: direct efficiency and numerical-representation predecessors cover substantial parts of the claim, the key aggregate table contains two unresolved contradictions, exact answers are intentionally penalized, probe baselines are weak, and pruning/layer comparisons are heavily confounded. The contribution should therefore be framed as an exploratory benchmark and hypothesis-generating audit rather than a mechanistic or cognitive conclusion.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text pass over all 24 pages of the exact indexed PDF, including every displayed table and figure, appendices A-G, method equations, limitation section, acknowledgments, and references. The cached PDF metadata identifies arXiv:2510.25776v1; the current official arXiv record was checked on 2026-08-23 and still lists only v1. Page anchors use PDF pages. Competitor titles, latest revision numbers, dates, and versioned URLs were checked against current official arXiv records on 2026-08-23. Author-reported results are separated from reviewer inference and contradiction audits; no formal theorem or proof appears in this empirical paper.
